title: Single Agent vs Multi-Agent Systems: An Architecture Decision Guide
excerpt: Compare single-agent and multi-agent architectures through task dependencies, coordination costs, error propagation, and a worked evaluation example.
content:
An AI agent architecture should follow the dependency structure of the work. A single agent keeps decisions and context together. A multi-agent system distributes work across separate decision loops, which can increase coverage or enforce boundaries, but also creates coordination work. The useful question is whether that additional work buys a measurable improvement for a particular task.

This guide develops an architecture decision using a hypothetical document-review service. The numbers illustrate how to reason about the choice; they are not benchmark results or product performance claims.

## Define what counts as a separate agent

Several model calls do not automatically make a multi-agent system. A deterministic pipeline that extracts fields, checks arithmetic in code, and drafts a response can have multiple calls without independent agents. Anthropic distinguishes predefined workflows from agents that dynamically choose their actions and tool use. That distinction helps keep architecture discussions precise. [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents).

For this decision, define an agent as a separately scoped execution loop with its own goal, context, tools, and stopping rule. Two prompts using the same unrestricted credentials and mutable transcript provide little meaningful isolation. Conversely, one user-facing assistant may route to several independently controlled workers.

Document three boundaries before choosing a framework: who owns each decision, what information each decision needs, and which component can change external state. These boundaries matter more than role names such as researcher, critic, or manager.

## Map dependencies before assigning roles

Start with a task graph. Each node should produce an artifact whose completion can be checked. Draw an edge only when the consumer actually needs the producer's result.

In our hypothetical service, a customer uploads a contract, an invoice, and a purchase order. The system must identify discrepancies and prepare a review packet. Contract extraction, invoice extraction, and purchase-order extraction can happen independently. Reconciliation depends on all three. Sending a payment instruction would depend on reconciliation and separate authorization.

The obvious parallel section is document extraction. Creating three agents to debate the final payment decision does not remove its dependencies. It may simply repeat the same evidence with different wording.

Consider three dimensions:

| Dimension | Favors one agent | Can justify multiple agents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evidence overlap | Every step needs the same small evidence set | Workers can inspect largely independent evidence |
| State ownership | One evolving plan with frequent revisions | Outputs can be handed off as stable artifacts |
| Authority | One narrow read-only capability set | Distinct permissions must be enforced |
| Verification | A shared validator can check the answer | Each specialist has a distinct checkable result |

These are design heuristics, not universal thresholds. A large document may justify separate extraction workers even when all workers use the same model. A short but sensitive task may need separation despite negligible parallelism.

## What published evidence actually supports

Anthropic's research-system account describes a lead agent coordinating parallel researchers, especially for questions with independent search directions. It also describes substantial token overhead and difficulty when tasks require tightly shared context. This supports investigating parallel exploration; it does not establish that a research architecture is best for every coding or transactional workflow. [How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/research/multi-agent-research-system).

A useful research caution comes from *Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems*. Its April 2026 revision evaluates 260 configurations across six benchmarks and reports that performance depends on task and coordination structure. The authors identify diminishing returns, tool-related coordination overhead, and error propagation differences. Benchmark-specific results should guide hypotheses, not become production promises. [Paper, version 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296v3).

Microsoft's architecture guidance adds organizational reasons for separation, including ownership and security boundaries, while acknowledging handoff latency and state-management costs. Separate agent prompts alone do not enforce these boundaries: deployment identity, tool authorization, and data access must do that work. [Single agent or multiple agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ai-agents/single-agent-multiple-agents).

## A worked decision with explicit assumptions

Assume the three extraction jobs each take 12 seconds, reconciliation takes 8 seconds, and final validation takes 4 seconds. Ignore queueing initially.

A sequential implementation takes 12 + 12 + 12 + 8 + 4 = 48 seconds. Three parallel extraction workers followed by reconciliation and validation take max(12, 12, 12) + 8 + 4 = 24 seconds before coordination overhead. If scheduling, handoff checks, and aggregation add 6 seconds, the total becomes 30 seconds.

That hypothetical improvement is useful only if the actual workload permits overlap. An API concurrency limit of one, a shared browser session, or document dependencies could erase it. Measure the real critical path rather than multiplying the number of workers by a nominal speedup. The implementation details belong in [parallel agent orchestration](/blog/parallel-agent-orchestration).

Now suppose each extraction job has a 0.95 probability of meeting its acceptance criteria. If all three must succeed and their failures were independent, the probability that every extraction succeeds would be 0.95 cubed, approximately 0.857. This calculation does not compare fairly against an unmeasured single-agent baseline. It demonstrates why individually strong worker scores do not establish end-to-end reliability. Shared OCR errors also violate the independence assumption.

Finally, assign illustrative costs of 4 units to each extraction, 3 to reconciliation, 2 to validation, and 3 to coordination. The parallel design costs 20 units per attempt. At an assumed 0.85 accepted-result rate, that is about 23.5 units per accepted result before retries. Compare that with the measured baseline's cost per accepted result, including human repair. A cheaper model call can still produce a more expensive workflow.

## Use contracts to contain coordination errors

In this example, each worker should return structured evidence rather than a confident narrative. A practical artifact might contain:

```json
{
  "task_id": "invoice-extraction-42",
  "input_version": "sha256:example",
  "status": "complete",
  "fields": {"currency": "USD", "total": "1250.00"},
  "evidence": [{"field": "total", "page": 2, "region": "footer"}],
  "uncertainties": []
}
```

This is an illustrative schema, not a complete production contract. Add tenant identity, schema version, timestamps, and access controls appropriate to the application. Reconciliation should reject incompatible input versions and missing required evidence. A worker's success status is a claim to validate, not permission to bypass checks.

Give one component ownership of the canonical review packet. Workers should propose updates or write separate artifacts rather than overwrite shared totals. A late result from a retried worker must not replace a newer accepted result. [Agent handoff contracts](/blog/agent-handoffs-shared-state) explains how ownership and versioned context reduce that ambiguity.

## Failure modes that change the decision

**Duplicate work:** two workers inspect the same document because the coordinator assigns vague objectives. Track input coverage and require explicit scope identifiers.

**Consensus without independence:** multiple agents share the same incorrect extraction, then agree. Preserve evidence provenance and introduce a validator with a different check, such as arithmetic or a source lookup. Agreement alone is not verification.

**Lossy handoffs:** a worker removes uncertainty when compressing its findings. Keep unresolved questions and evidence references as mandatory fields. Limit summary length without deleting the ability to inspect supporting material.

**Coordinator overload:** the lead agent receives long transcripts from every worker. Return bounded artifacts and store detailed traces separately. If aggregation needs every raw transcript, the proposed decomposition may not be saving useful context.

**Split authority:** two agents can approve or execute the same action. Move mutation authorization into application code and give it a stable action identity. Separate reasoning roles should not create duplicate payment rights.

## Run an architecture experiment that can falsify the proposal

Build a representative evaluation set containing straightforward cases, conflicting documents, missing pages, malicious instructions inside documents, and timeouts. Keep the same tools, evidence access, model capability, and task acceptance criteria across variants. Otherwise the experiment measures several changes at once.

Compare a single-agent baseline, a deterministic extraction pipeline, and the proposed coordinated system. Record accepted-result rate, critical errors, human repair time, cost per accepted result, and latency distributions. Count failed and abandoned runs. Review outcomes by task category so an overall average does not hide regressions on sensitive cases.

Add fault injection: delay one worker, return an outdated artifact, remove a required field, and fail the coordinator after workers complete. The expected behavior should be written before running the experiment. For example, a missing purchase order should produce an incomplete review packet rather than an invented reconciliation.

Choose the simpler design when the measured benefit is too small to pay for monitoring, migrations, and recovery. Choose multiple agents when they satisfy a concrete requirement that the baseline cannot, and retain the evidence supporting that decision.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a multi-agent system require different models?

No. Separate loops can use the same model with different evidence and permissions. Different models may add diversity, but they also introduce additional evaluation and operational requirements.

### Should every specialist be an autonomous agent?

No. If extraction follows a fixed contract, a bounded model call with a validator may be sufficient. Reserve autonomous loops for work that benefits from choosing subsequent actions.

### Can I add multiple agents later?

Yes, if the initial system already separates task state, tool contracts, evidence, and execution ownership. Stable interfaces make it easier to replace one bounded step with a worker without redesigning the whole service.
